Compounding 101

What does a compounding pharmacy actually do?

Most pharmacies count and label medicines made in a factory. A compounding pharmacy also makes medicines, one prescription at a time. Here's what that means, who it helps, and how it's regulated.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 18, 2026

Compounding in one sentence

Compounding is when a pharmacist prepares a medication for a specific patient, from a prescription, because a commercially made product doesn't meet that patient's needs.

Who it helps

  • People who need a strength that isn't made, such as low-dose naltrexone, which is usually 0.5 to 4.5 mg.
  • People who can't swallow pills, who may do better with a liquid, a troche or a rapid-dissolve tablet.
  • People with allergies or sensitivities to dyes, fillers or preservatives.
  • Hormone therapy patients whose clinicians order a specific combination or form.
  • Pets, who need tiny doses, flavors like chicken or tuna, or a gel instead of a pill.
  • Anyone whose medicine has been discontinued or is hard to find, when compounding is appropriate.

Nonsterile and sterile compounding

Nonsterile compounding makes things like capsules, creams, liquids, troches and treats. It follows the national standard USP <795>. Sterile compounding makes preparations that must be free of germs, like injections and eye drops. It's done in a certified clean room under USP <797>. Pharmacies that handle hazardous drugs also follow USP <800>. We do nonsterile and select sterile compounding.

How it's regulated

  • State boards of pharmacy license and inspect pharmacies. In Florida, sterile compounding requires a special permit.
  • Federal law allows pharmacies like ours (called 503A pharmacies) to compound for individual patients with a prescription. Larger "outsourcing facilities" (503B) register with the FDA and make batches for offices and hospitals.
  • Compounded medications are not FDA-approved. The FDA doesn't review each compounded preparation before it's made, which is why a pharmacy's own standards matter so much.

What happens to your prescription

  1. Your prescriber or veterinarian sends the prescription.
  2. A pharmacist reviews the formula, the dose and your history.
  3. We make it in our lab with ingredients from established suppliers, each lot arriving with a certificate of analysis.
  4. A pharmacist checks the finished preparation, labels it with a beyond-use date and storage directions, and we call you.

Most compounds are ready the same day or within 24 hours.

Not all compounding pharmacies are alike. Ask any compounding pharmacy whether it's accredited, which USP standards it meets, where its ingredients come from, and whether sterile batches are tested by an outside lab. We wrote a full guide to choosing a compounding pharmacy.

How we do it

Pharmacy on the Park is accredited by The Compliance Team and USP <800> compliant, and we meet USP <795> and <797>. Pharmetric Labs, an independent laboratory, tests every sterile batch. We exceed Florida's compounding standards, and a pharmacist answers when you call.

Common questions

Is compounding legal?

Yes. Compounding is a long-standing part of pharmacy practice, regulated by state boards of pharmacy and federal law. Pharmacies like ours compound from a prescription for an individual patient.

Does insurance pay for compounded medications?

It depends on your plan, and many plans don't. We'll tell you the price before we make your prescription.

Can I ask for a compounded medication myself?

A compounded medication needs a prescription. Talk with your prescriber or veterinarian, and they can send it to us or call to discuss options with a pharmacist.

This article is general information and not medical advice. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved and are not commercially manufactured products. Your prescriber decides whether a compounded medication is right for you.
